notes: Domicile dispute over playwright Anthony Shaffer's estate; detailed factual findings support enrichment.

enrichment.short_title: Anthony Shaffer domicile at death for IHT and 1975 Act claims

statutes_considered.title: Inheritance (Provision for Family and Dependents) Act 1975

key_facts: Playwright Anthony Shaffer died in London in November 2001; his domicile of origin was England and Wales.
His widow Diane Cilento and daughters contended he died domiciled in Queensland; Marie Josette Capece Minutolo contended he remained or revived an English domicile.
From 1975 Shaffer followed Cilento to Australia, married at Karnak in Queensland, built 'The Castle', and treated Karnak as his home while retaining a London studio for work and medical treatment.
From the mid-1990s he spent increasing time in London, formed a relationship with Jo, and separated from Diane after she discovered the affair shortly before his death.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial to determine domicile at death affecting inheritance tax liability and eligibility for claims under the 1975 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Held that Anthony Shaffer died domiciled in Queensland; his domicile of choice was not abandoned before death.
enrichment.ratio: A domicile of choice requires voluntary residence with intention to remain indefinitely; abandonment requires cessation of residence and an unequivocal absence of intention to return, and a withering intention to return does not suffice if the propositus dies before it is lost.
legal_issues: Whether Anthony Shaffer acquired a domicile of choice in Queensland
Whether he abandoned that domicile before death so that his domicile of origin revived
Relevance of matrimonial home, tax planning, dual residences, and late-life relationships to domicile
linked_authorities: Udny v Udny (1869) 1 LR Sc & Div 441
Re Flynn [1968] 1 WLR 103
IRC v Bullock [1976] 1 WLR 1178
In the Estate of Fuld (No 3)

confidence.notes: Detailed first-instance judgment with clear legal framework and explicit conclusion on domicile at death.

notes: Ship sale 'subject details' construction; expedited Commercial Court trial with agreed no-appeal terms.

enrichment.short_title: Ship sale recap 'subject details' and binding contract
key_facts: Thoresen agreed broker terms to buy three vessels en bloc for US$42 million less commission from Efshipping-managed sellers.
Brokers Straume and Kokkinis had full authority; the recap email included clause 10 on Norwegian Saleform 1993 'sub details suitably amended'.
Sellers insisted on retaining 'sub details' after Thoresen's broker sought to delete it; post-recap MOA drafting disputes continued until sellers declared negotiations failed.
Parties agreed to forgo appeal and that sellers would abide by the court's decision if a binding contract was found.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited Commercial Court trial on whether email exchanges on 27–28 November 2003 constituted a binding contract for sale of three vessels.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no binding contract for sale of the vessels was concluded.
enrichment.ratio: In ship sale negotiations, 'subject details' is a recognised maritime variant of 'subject to contract' meaning there is no binding agreement until all details of the proposed formal agreement are agreed, and that meaning is not displaced where the recap also records agreed main terms.
legal_issues: Construction of 'sub details' in clause 10 of the recap email
Whether main terms agreed on price and delivery created a binding contract despite pending NSF amendments
Effect of broker negotiations before and after the recap on contract formation

notes: Prison Rules cash account trust issue; Court of Appeal unanimous dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Prisoners' cash under rule 43(3) and trust status
key_facts: Life prisoner Duggan challenged whether cash paid into a governor-controlled account under Prison Rule 43(3) is held on trust.
Prisoners must surrender cash on reception; credits are recorded in prison books and managed through the PIES internal banking system.
Aggregate prisoners' monies in Prison Service accounts exceeded £4.7 million nationally.
The appeal raised whether rule 43(3) creates a trustee/beneficiary relationship or a debtor/creditor banker/customer relationship.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Hart J on whether Prison Rule 43(3) imposes a trust on prisoners' cash paid into a governor-controlled account.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; rule 43(3) does not impose a trust and the relationship is debtor/creditor rather than trustee/beneficiary.
enrichment.ratio: Rule 43(3) transfers possession and ownership of prisoners' cash to the prison authorities without language or circumstances implying a trust; crediting the prisoner in prison books indicates a banker/customer debtor/creditor relationship, not fiduciary trusteeship.
legal_issues: Whether Prison Rule 43(3) creates an express or implied trust of prisoners' cash
Distinction between bailment of chattels under rule 43(2) and treatment of fungible cash under rule 43(3)
Whether interference with prisoners' possessions under Article 1 Protocol 1 ECHR is proportionate

Joachimson v Swiss Bank Corporation [1921] 3 KB 110
Hazell v Hammersmith and Fulham London Borough Council [1992] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Unanimous Court of Appeal with detailed analysis of rule 43 and banking/trust principles.

notes: Complex fact-finding on shaken baby and hospital airway incidents; treating doctors' evidence required careful judicial scrutiny.

enrichment.short_title: Care proceedings after shaken baby and hospital airway incidents
key_facts: Local authority applied for a care order for baby Cade after bilateral subdural haematomas were discovered following three hospital admissions in July 2002.
The father admitted shaking Cade on 30 July 2002; the parents separated and Cade was returned to the mother during the hearing.
The authority alleged additional non-accidental injuries and that the father deliberately obstructed Cade's airway on seven of ten hospital deterioration episodes.
After a four-day fact-finding hearing the judge found threshold proved by the shaking and by deliberate airway obstruction on 2 and 4 August 2002.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Supplementary fact-finding hearing in public law care proceedings after father admitted one shaking incident and threshold was already established.
enrichment.outcome: Threshold criteria found proved because of the father's shaking on 30 July 2002 and deliberate airway obstruction causing collapse on 2 and 4 August 2002; mother not involved.
enrichment.ratio: Where a treating specialist has been closely involved in a child's hospital care, the court may rely on their conclusions if it gives due weight to the risks of emotional involvement and initial impression bias, especially where supported by independent expert and nursing evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the father caused minor injuries and deliberate airway obstruction in hospital
Admissibility and weight of treating doctors' evidence in care proceedings
Whether further fact-finding was necessary despite existing threshold admission
linked_authorities: Re B (Sexual Abuse: Expert's Report) [2001] 1 FLR 871

confidence.notes: Outcome and principal findings are clear, but the judgment itself emphasises caution in relying on treating specialists and only two of ten alleged hospital incidents were found proved.

notes: Parole Board recall fairness and witness attendance; judicial review appeal dismissed.

enrichment.short_title: Parole Board recall hearing without alleged victim
key_facts: Life licensee Brooks was recalled after his partner Shirley Langhorne alleged rape and domestic violence to probation officers.
Langhorne made a police statement asserting the rape but refused to give evidence in court or before the Parole Board.
The Parole Board confirmed recall at an oral hearing relying on probation and police account evidence without Langhorne's oral testimony.
Brooks sought judicial review arguing unfairness and that the Secretary of State should have secured Langhorne's attendance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal from dismissal of judicial review of Parole Board decisions refusing release after licence revocation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Parole Board process was fair and it was entitled to find the rape allegation proved on the evidence before it.
enrichment.ratio: Parole Board proceedings are not criminal trials; where abundant untested but admissible evidence supports recall, absence of the alleged victim does not necessarily vitiate fairness, especially where the licensee's solicitors chose to proceed without seeking an adjournment or witness summons.
legal_issues: Whether recall proceedings were unfair without the alleged victim's oral evidence
Responsibility for securing witness attendance before the Parole Board
Standard and quality of evidence sufficient to justify continued detention on licence recall

confidence.notes: Detailed Court of Appeal judgment with clear outcome and guidance on witness attendance practice before the Parole Board.

notes: Anonymised employment appeal on covert video admissibility; section 39 order continued.

enrichment.short_title: Covert home video admissibility in sex discrimination claim
key_facts: Nanny X claimed constructive dismissal and sex discrimination, alleging unwanted sexual advances by employer Y while working in the home of Y and Z.
Y and Z denied harassment and contended there was a consensual sexual relationship; X secretly filmed Y in the kitchen, also capturing child J.
The Employment Tribunal viewed the video and held it had no probative value and should not be admitted, balancing Article 6 and Article 8.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal held the video potentially relevant and ordered private viewing; Y and Z appealed to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employers' appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal decision that covert video evidence was potentially admissible in Employment Tribunal sex discrimination proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; video held irrelevant on the pleaded case and inadmissible; employers awarded costs summarily assessed at £5,000.
enrichment.ratio: Covert video evidence is inadmissible if irrelevant to the issues as pleaded; where the dispute is whether conduct was consensual throughout, timing of filming after an alleged end to consent does not assist unless the case is pleaded on that basis, and a tribunal that has viewed the video is entitled to deference on demeanour.
legal_issues: Relevance and admissibility of covertly recorded video evidence
Balance between Article 6 fair trial and Article 8 private life
Whether Employment Appeal Tribunal could overturn tribunal finding of no probative value without viewing the video
linked_authorities: Jones v University of Warwick

confidence.notes: Parties anonymised by court order but legal issues and outcome are fully stated in the judgment.

notes: Libel Part 36 settlement costs for unilateral statement in open court; short Eady J ruling.

enrichment.short_title: Libel Part 36 acceptance and costs of open court statement
key_facts: Claimant Phillipps accepted a Part 36 offer in libel proceedings against Associated Newspapers after the defendant paid money into court.
The defendant refused a joint statement but an apology was published; the claimant sought permission for a unilateral statement in open court.
The defendant objected in principle and on wording, then did not oppose permission at the hearing but contested costs.
The defendant argued CPR 36.13 stopped the costs clock at acceptance so the claimant should bear statement costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to read a unilateral statement in open court following Part 36 acceptance, with dispute over costs of preparation and the hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; established practice unchanged so defendant pays costs of the Part 23 application and unilateral statement as part of action costs.
enrichment.ratio: Acceptance of a Part 36 offer or payment in defamation proceedings does not alter the long-established practice that a defendant who pays into court will normally bear the incidental costs of a claimant's unilateral statement in open court, whether the Part 23 application is made before or after acceptance.
legal_issues: Interaction of CPR 36.13 with Part 53 Practice Direction on statements in open court
Whether costs of a unilateral libel statement continue after Part 36 acceptance
Court discretion over costs where a defendant objects to statement wording

notes: Pension scheme s.75 summary judgment application; complex statutory scheme but clear dispositive conclusions.

enrichment.short_title: Pension scheme winding-up debt and gilts-matching consultation

statutes_considered.title: Occupational Pension Schemes (Minimum Funding Requirement and Actuarial Valuations) Regulations 1996
Occupational Pension Schemes (Deficiency on Winding-up etc) Regulations 1996

key_facts: Trustees of the merged BETEC/Roxspur pension plan sought £4,409,003 from Roxspur under section 75 after winding-up left a final salary deficit.
Money purchase benefits from the Roxspur scheme had been transferred into the BETEC plan by deed and transfer agreement in 1999.
Trustees purported to adopt a gilts-matching investment policy on 29 May 2003 without prior consultation, then certified the deficiency.
Roxspur applied for summary dismissal arguing invalid consultation and that the plan should be treated as separate schemes for deficiency purposes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-applications for summary judgment on whether an employer debt under section 75 Pensions Act 1995 had been validly established after scheme winding-up.
enrichment.outcome: Trustees' claim summarily dismissed; plan treated as single scheme but actuary's certificate invalid for failure to consult employer before revising investment principles.
enrichment.ratio: Prior consultation with the employer is a precondition to validly revising a statement of investment principles under section 35(5)(b); without it a gilts-matching based section 75 valuation certificate is invalid and the debt is not established, though trustees may seek a fresh valid certificate within the applicable time period.
legal_issues: Whether merged final salary and money purchase plan is a single scheme for section 75
Whether section 75(1B) and Deficiency Regulations require separate treatment of benefit elements
Whether trustees validly consulted the employer before adopting a gilts-matching policy
Meaning of 'applicable time' in section 75(3) for ascertaining the debt

notes: Certificate of inadequacy application; Lightman J declined to follow unapproved note of Collins J and left final certificate form open for further argument.

enrichment.short_title: Confiscation certificate of inadequacy and hidden assets
key_facts: O'Donoghue sought a certificate of inadequacy after realisations fell short of values attributed to his car and caravan in a £94,587 confiscation order.
Prosecution accepted a £11,100 shortfall on those items if overall realisable property had not increased, but disputed adequacy because of £35,500 withdrawn from a third party's account.
The defendant could not go behind the original finding that he beneficially owned the £35,500 and failed to disclose what had happened to it.
Counsel relied on an unapproved note of Collins J in Re Turner suggesting interest on retained cash should not be assumed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for a certificate of inadequacy under the Criminal Justice Act 1988 confiscation regime opposing the prosecutor.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused for failure to discharge the burden of proving inadequacy; court left open whether to refuse any certificate or allow one subject to a presumed return on the £35,500.
enrichment.ratio: On an application for a certificate of inadequacy the defendant bears the burden of showing what has happened to realisable assets found at the confiscation hearing; speculation about interest on hidden assets does not discharge that burden, and Article 6 does not exempt hidden assets from that principle.
legal_issues: Burden of proof on a defendant applying for a certificate of inadequacy
Whether possible interest or fruits of hidden assets must be offset against shortfalls on other assets
Whether Article 6 requires a different approach where assets were 'hidden'
Effect of unapproved judicial note in Re Turner
linked_authorities: Gokal v SFO [2001] EWCA Civ 368
Phillips v UK (Application No 41087/98)

confidence.notes: Core legal principles are clearly stated but final relief on the certificate amount was expressly left open pending further argument.

notes: Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 s.11(1A) sublease installation scope; damages reduced on appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Sublessor liability for water supply under section 11
key_facts: Niazi held a head lease of a top-floor Chelsea flat and sublet to Van Der Loo at £34,800 per annum.
Water pressure failures for 33 months were caused by works to restaurant premises below installing a larger take-off pipe outside the demised flat.
The county court awarded £48,000 damages largely by a 40% notional rent abatement for water and lighting failures.
Niazi appealed arguing section 11(1A) did not extend liability to installations in parts of the building outside its demise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from county court counterclaim for breach of implied repairing covenants under section 11 Landlord and Tenant Act 1985.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; sublessor not liable for inadequate water supply or common-part lighting; damages reduced to £9,050 for admitted breaches.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 11(1A)(b)(i), a sublessor's implied covenant to repair installations serving the dwelling extends only to installations forming part of a part of the building in which the lessor has an estate or interest, not to defective pipework in parts of the building outside the demise.
legal_issues: Scope of section 11(1A) where a dwelling forms part only of a building
Whether a sublessor is liable for water and electricity installations outside the demised flat
Appropriate measure of damages for disrepair where tenant remains in occupation
